title: Why Do Some Leaders Feel More Stress?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This post explains why some leaders experience more stress than others and then names a remedy. It defines stress as the body's response to real or perceived demands and notes that intense, frequent or prolonged stress damages decision making, productivity and accuracy. Differences in stress are attributed to inborn nervous system reactivity, past experience such as trauma or unpredictability, feelings of powerlessness, and poor sleep and downtime. For leaders in particular, a high need for control raises stress because perfectionism makes every choice a potential threat. The author's answer is optimism, defined as a disciplined belief that progress is possible and opportunity exists in any challenge. The post adds that optimism is a learned skill, so the way stress is experienced can be changed.
points: Chronic stress is linked to errors, irritability and weak decisions, so it is a performance issue and not just a comfort issue.
Stress varies by biology, past exposure to unpredictability, powerlessness and lack of rest.
A leader's high need for control is singled out as a specific amplifier of stress.
Optimism is presented as the regulator that separates leaders who handle stress well.
The post claims optimism is learnable, meaning stress response can be changed through mindset.
quotes: Stress is the body’s natural response to demands, pressures, and challenges, whether they come from real situations or perceived circumstances.

Stress becomes harmful when it’s intense, frequent, or long-lasting. When leaders are in that state, it affects nearly every system in the body and mind, producing fatigue, worry, irritability, poor concentration, and an inability to make sharp decisions.
Some people are born with more reactive nervous systems and a brain chemistry that can make stress responses stronger and more long-lasting.
Past exposure to unpredictable situations makes modest challenges more threatening. Stress worsens when people feel powerless or trapped. Lack of sleep and limited downtime also amplify stress.
Optimism is the magic bullet. The disciplined belief that progress is always possible and opportunity exists in any challenge regulates feelings of stress.
And here’s the good news: Research has proven that optimism is a learned skill. How stress is experienced and managed can be changed with an optimistic mindset.
